items.title: Build shared workflows for your team with Copilot Automations
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Shared Copilot Automations are rolling out, enabling teams to build and maintain AI-powered workflows together. With Copilot Automations, you can combine prompts, triggers, and tools to design workflows around the way your team works. Copilot runs autonomously in the cloud, using only the tools you’ve allowed. For example, you could create automations to: Reproduce bugs as soon as an issue is opened. Capture screenshots of the changes when a pull request is marked as ready. Automatically investigate production incidents as soon as they’re detected in your monitoring tool. Until now, automations have been personal, meaning only you could see and edit them, and they used your identity and AI credits. That works well for automating your own work, like drafting your standup updates, but not for workflows your whole team relies on. Shared automations let your team build and maintain those workflows together. How shared automations work Visible to your team: Everyone with read access to the repository can see a shared automation, and anyone with write access can edit it. Billed to the repository owner: AI credits are billed to the organization or user that owns the repository, rather than to the person who created the automation. Act as Copilot: Actions on GitHub are attributed to Copilot, rather than to any one user. Built to last: Shared automations belong to the repository, so they keep running if the person who created them leaves the team. Change history lets your team see how the tools, triggers, and prompt have evolved. For shared automations to run in an organization-owned repository, an administrator must enable the “Allow use of Copilot cloud agent billed to the organization” policy. Create a shared automation When you create an automation on github.com, the GitHub Copilot app , or Visual Studio Code, choose Shared under Type. You can’t change an automation’s type after you create it. To learn more, see personal and shared automations. Shared Copilot Automations
items.why_it_matters: Shared Copilot Automations run agents in the cloud from triggers, for example to reproduce bugs or investigate incidents. This is relevant to the gated agent pipelines we set up for clients.

items.title: Generate and edit images directly in Copilot
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: You can now generate and edit images using natural language in GitHub Copilot. When you ask for an image, your selected reasoning model calls a dedicated image-generation tool powered by GPT Image 2.5 Flare, previews the result inline, and saves it to your project. Previously, getting a visual asset while working in Copilot meant stepping away to a separate tool, describing what you needed again, generating it there, and manually bringing it back into your project. This update removes that context switch, so you can go from an idea to a usable image without breaking your flow. Describe an image conversationally in any Copilot chat session, whether you’re starting a new request or in the middle of a coding task. Copilot previews the generated image inline and saves it directly to your workspace. Organization and enterprise owners can turn off image generation by disabling the image generation model using Copilot model policies. You can opt in to a visible “Made with AI” watermark on images Copilot generates and edits. Watermarking is off by default. To try it, open a Copilot chat in VS Code, the GitHub Copilot app, or Copilot CLI and describe the image you want. Image generation is in public preview for Copilot Pro, Copilot Pro+, Copilot Business, and Copilot Enterprise. It’s billed separately from your chat model, based on image tokens that count toward your plan’s AI credits. Join the discussion within GitHub Community. The post Generate and edit images directly in Copilot appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: Copilot can now generate and edit images inline using GPT Image 2.5 Flare. Handy for MVP placeholder assets, but it is not core to how we deliver code.

items.title: GitHub Agentic Workflows generally available
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: GitHub Agentic Workflows, an open source project from GitHub Next, is now generally available. With agentic workflows, you can automate reasoning-based tasks like issue triage, CI failure analysis, documentation updates, and test writing by using coding agents inside GitHub Actions. Define your automation in natural language Markdown files, and GitHub Agentic Workflows compiles them into standard Actions YAML. Because these are GitHub Actions, they reuse your existing runner groups and policy constraints. You can use GitHub Copilot or bring your own coding agent to power each workflow. We’ve been rolling out our agentic developer workflows, and the results are measurable. One of our leads saved an estimated 29 hours a week on his development work alone. Across his team, measured velocity has more than doubled on average, and AI now authors 91% of the team’s commits. With these workflows, the team cut production errors from about 11,000 a day to under 1,000 and drove a technology migration end to end. One workflow takes a feature from requirements to implementation with validation evidence. Others keep our frameworks current and steadily raise code quality and test coverage. Because AI drives the process to completion, our engineers can run four or five efforts in parallel and stay focused on the bigger goals. Ben Alton – Senior manager, Strategy, Architecture & Innovation team at Accenture Built-in safeguards GitHub Agentic Workflows incorporates layered safeguards for your automation. Agents access GitHub content respecting the integrity filter rules, run with read-only permissions by default, and execute inside a sandboxed container behind the Agent Workflow Firewall. The outputs are validated through the safe outputs process, and a dedicated threat detection job scans all proposed changes before they are applied. Additional capabilities for general availability Highlights since the public preview include: Actions Runner Controller (ARC) and Docker-in-Docker suppo
items.why_it_matters: GitHub Agentic Workflows is now GA. It compiles natural-language Markdown into Actions YAML and supports bring-your-own coding agent, so it plugs straight into our GitHub Actions and agent review pipelines.

items.title: GitHub Copilot app, Universe releases
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Work doesn’t always fit in a single repository or session. A feature can span several repositories. A launch plan can pull in specs, designs, and assets without touching a repository at all. Projects in the GitHub Copilot app give that work one home, with its context, agents, and results together. Copilot coordinates the work in the background and checks in when it needs you. Give Copilot a goal Start a project, describe what you want to get done, and add the context Copilot needs (e.g., repositories, design mocks, Slack threads, or notes from a design meeting). Choose the models and tools for the job. Copilot runs as many agents as the work needs and brings back results (e.g., pull requests) for your review. Use project automations for repeatable tasks, such as creating a new promo video whenever a feature lands. For a focused task in a single repository, you can still start a session directly from that repository. Copilot Projects are now in public preview. You can learn more in the projects documentation. Handle the work around your code Use context from connected tools such as Slack and Figma to research a request, draft a specification, or work through a design alongside your code. You can also generate and edit images using natural language in chat. Let Copilot work with your desktop apps Ask Copilot to work through tasks in your desktop apps, such as an expense-report workflow. Computer use—in public preview on macOS and Windows—lets Copilot read app content, click controls, enter or edit text, and navigate across apps, including those without an API, command-line interface, or MCP integration. Copilot asks for your approval before controlling an app, and your organization can disable the feature through managed settings. To get started, open Settings > Computer Use and turn on Enable Computer Use. On macOS, grant the required Accessibility and Screen Recording permissions. For more information, see the computer use documentation. Get started Download or upda
items.why_it_matters: Copilot app projects coordinate agents across multiple repos and outside context. A useful comparison point for our Claude Code and Codex multi-repo workflows, and relevant to clients standardized on Copilot.

items.title: GitHub Copilot Fusion now supports selection of local models
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Today we are shipping intelligent routing for local models into experimental preview. GitHub Copilot Fusion can now choose between supported on-device models and cloud models, enabling intelligent local model routing in GitHub Copilot CLI, GitHub Copilot app, and Visual Studio Code. This opt-in experimental preview lets you use your device’s compute without switching models manually for each request. For a deeper dive into this feature, see our original announcement on October 7th. Managed download and setup on Windows On supported Windows devices, you can download and configure MAI Code 1.1 Flash through the Windows ML provider. In Copilot CLI, enable experimental mode and open /model to follow the setup prompts. In the Copilot app, configure the Windows ML provider under Settings > Model providers, enable Local model auto routing under Settings > Experiments, and start a new session. Windows ML local models is enabled by default on Windows. In VS Code, enable chat.copilot.localModel.enabled. Once the model is ready, select Standard in Copilot Fusion to let Copilot choose between local and cloud models. You can also select the local model directly for your session. Bring your own local model The managed download experience is Windows-only, but Copilot CLI’s local Copilot Fusion routing also works with manually configured models on Windows, macOS, and Linux. You can configure MAI Code 1.1 Flash or Qwen3.8 Flash Next through a local OpenAI-compatible server. You manage the model download and inference runtime, and your device must have sufficient resources to run it. Configure the model as a supported local-model provider, enable experimental local routing, and select Standard in Copilot Fusion to let Copilot choose between eligible local and cloud models. This builds on the recent local-model discovery improvements in Copilot CLI. Adding or discovering a model through bring your own key (BYOK) configuration doesn’t automatically make it eligible for Copilot Fusion.
items.why_it_matters: Copilot Fusion can now route requests between local on-device models and cloud models. This is an experimental preview, mostly on Windows, so near-term impact on our workflow is limited.

Keep work moving without staying at your desk or in one tool. With GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio Code, start a cloud agent session from your phone at standup, steer it from VS Code at your desk, and check on it from github.com at lunch. Session continuity lets you pick up the same session across these clients while your agent keeps working in the cloud. Start and follow cloud sessions across Copilot clients Hand off work without keeping your computer on. Start a cloud agent session from the Agents window in VS Code. The work runs on GitHub’s infrastructure, so closing your laptop doesn’t stop it. Find and continue the same session in VS Code, the GitHub Copilot app, GitHub Mobile, github.com, or Copilot CLI. Sessions started in a Slack or Microsoft Teams DM can also be continued in these clients. Keep agents working on your own machines Move on to another task or project without worrying about losing your session. The new Agent Host isolates your Copilot sessions from individual VS Code windows, so work continues in the background after you close the project folder or window. You can also run agents on a separate machine while you use your primary development machine for other work. The power and flexibility of VS Code’s Remote SSH and dev tunnels extends to the Agents window. The remote agent works with the same code, tools, and dependencies, and can keep running when you disconnect or quit VS Code locally. The remote machine and its Agent Host must remain running. Move between the editor and Agents windows Switch between the editor and the Agents window without starting over. Both views stay in sync with the same live Copilot session. Control agents on your machine from your phone Check progress, give direction, or start a new task on your development machine from GitHub Mobile. Your ph
items.why_it_matters: Copilot in VS Code adds cloud agent sessions that continue across phone, editor and web, plus wider model choice. Useful context for engineers on Copilot-based client teams.

items.title: GitHub Enterprise now includes access to GitHub Copilot
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Enterprises working with a GitHub or Microsoft account team can now get Copilot included with GitHub Enterprise for every licensed user. Previously, you had to manage two things: how many Copilot seats you were paying for and how much AI usage those users consumed. With Copilot included in the platform, usage against your enterprise budget is the primary thing to manage. Self-serve availability is coming in stages, and current self-serve subscriptions are unaffected. Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise remain available. Users in your enterprise account who do not hold a GitHub Enterprise license get the same Copilot access through Copilot Standalone, at $10 per user per month. Copilot access through GitHub Enterprise and Copilot Standalone has the same features and models as Copilot Enterprise but does not include monthly AI credits per seat. What you manage AI usage is metered from the first request against your enterprise budget, using the policies, alerts, and attribution you already have. There is no included usage allowance to track or top up. To learn more, review our documentation on Copilot billing for enterprises. Code completion and next edit suggestions keep working even with no budget available. Copilot Chat, Copilot code review, and Copilot in the cloud require available budget to use. An exhausted budget never removes access. The seat and the features that don’t need budget stay. Availability If you work with a GitHub or Microsoft account team: Available now for GitHub Enterprise Cloud. Talk to your sales team about setting up a new enterprise account on this model or transitioning an existing enterprise account. If you manage your own subscription: Currently unavailable. We are opening this to self-serve customers in stages and will share dates in the coming weeks. Your current subscription is unaffected. Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise: Both remain available to purchase for new and existing enterprises. To learn more, check out our update
items.why_it_matters: Copilot is now bundled with GitHub Enterprise and billed by usage instead of seats. This changes how enterprise clients buy AI coding tools and may shape tool choice on staff augmentation work.

items.title: GitHub intelligence puts your code, context, and history to work
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Agents should understand more than your codebase—they should understand how your team works. Your preferences, repository conventions, skills, and custom instructions guide how changes should be made, while code in related repositories can show how the pieces fit together. Without that context, agents spend time rediscovering knowledge and can miss your team’s conventions. GitHub intelligence is the context and learning layer sourced from the graph of GitHub data. It makes this data useful to agents, helping them remember how you work, keep that guidance current, and find the code and development history relevant to the next task. The goal is for agents to build on what you and your team already know, rather than treating every session as a fresh start. That is the advantage of building where your team’s work already lives. A repository memory can capture why an edge case matters and which test covers it. GitHub intelligence allows agents to use that context, with controls over what they can access. Three capabilities bring this into your workflow: Memory carries knowledge between sessions Dreaming keeps the context current Code search reaches beyond your checkout. Availability and settings vary by capability. Memory: Pick up where you left off GitHub Copilot Memory is now generally available on paid Copilot plans. Copilot can remember personal preferences and repository conventions across sessions and clients. Memories can be created in the Copilot app, Copilot CLI, VS Code, Copilot cloud agent, Copilot code review, Slack, Teams, and GitHub Mobile. You can tell Copilot, Remember to start my pull request descriptions with a TL;DR, and it can reuse that preference across Copilot experiences. Repository memories can capture the right test command or how your team expects Copilot to check its work, so you spend less time repeating guidance in each session. Copilot sessions autonomously generate and curate memories, learning from every interaction. Among the Copilot CLI
items.why_it_matters: GitHub intelligence is a context and memory layer for agents, built from repo conventions, skills and instructions. It is directly analogous to our CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md context engineering practice.

items.title: Route and orchestrate models with GitHub Copilot Fusion
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: GitHub Copilot Fusion is generally available. Instead of picking a model for each task, choose Copilot Fusion and let Copilot intelligently route and orchestrate which models it uses for you. Copilot Fusion brings together Project HydraFusion’s multi-model orchestration and Copilot auto model selection’s fine-tuned model selection, leveraging the benefits of both to balance performance and cost efficiency. Since Project HydraFusion launched, we’ve improved its performance. In the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Copilot Fusion Max scored 60, within two points of Claude Code with Opus 5.5 Max. It delivered that result at about half the average API cost per task, using about half as many tokens and taking about 40% less time per task. Smarter choices for developers When you select Copilot Fusion in the model picker, you aren’t selecting a specific model. You’re choosing a system that routes and orchestrates models for each task. There’s no need to switch models during a task or decide which model suits each step. For each prompt, Copilot Fusion determines which models to use and how they work together, while you choose the right level of effort. To use it, select Copilot Fusion in the model picker, then choose the effort level. Fusion Standard: Prioritizes versatile models for everyday coding. Fusion High: Prioritizes capable models for challenging tasks and deeper reasoning. Fusion Max: Prioritizes the most capable models for the most demanding tasks and complex reasoning. Watch as Copilot Fusion analyzes each task and selects a model to complete it, orchestrating multiple models through the following workflows when needed. Single: One model solves the task directly. Cascade: An efficient model drafts a response. A quality check determines whether to accept it or escalate to a stronger model. Critique: One model drafts an initial response, another model reviews it, and the original model revises. More control for administrators Administrators control which mod
items.why_it_matters: Copilot Fusion is now generally available with automatic multi-model routing, scoring near Claude Code with Opus 5 on a coding agent index. A notable competitor option for client teams on Copilot.

items.title: Security extension for the GitHub Copilot app
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: You can now work through your repository’s GitHub code scanning alerts without leaving the GitHub Copilot app. The new GitHub security extension, now in public preview, lets you find the alerts that matter most and ask Copilot to explain or help fix them. Until now, fixing a code scanning alert meant switching between the alert on github.com and the code in your editor. With the security extension, you can move from finding an alert to fixing it in one place. Fix the alerts already in your code If you already run code scanning on your repository, the security extension shows its open code scanning alerts: Browse every open code scanning alert, ordered by severity, and use search and filters to narrow the list. Open an alert to see its details and the affected code. You can open the full alert page on github.com when you need more context. Select one or more alerts and ask Copilot to Explain or Fix them. Copilot only makes fixes in your local working copy and doesn’t commit or push anything. This way you can review and iterate on the changes in the app and push when you’re ready. See linked pull requests on an alert so you know whether someone is already working on a fix. Dismiss alerts you don’t plan to fix. If your organization uses delegated alert dismissal, the extension sends your dismissal for approval. Catch new issues before you open a pull request Run /security-review on your current changes and see those findings next to your existing alerts. The extension tells you when your code has changed since the last review so you know when to run it again. You can also ask Copilot about your alerts in chat. Copilot uses the security extension’s tools in the same way as any other tool, following your tool permission settings. Get started To install the security extension: In your terminal run copilot plugin install github-security@awesome-copilot. In the GitHub Copilot app, click Customize, search for github-security, then click + Install. The extension is automatica
items.why_it_matters: A public preview extension lets the Copilot app explain and fix code scanning alerts in one place. This fits our no-compromise security stance on GitHub-hosted client repos.

items.title: [AINews] Anthropic ends Coding Interviews: "Hunger beats tenure"
items.author: swyx .ai
items.excerpt: Several midsize headlines today; on top of some impressive Math verification, Google Genie and Artificial Analysis and FrontierCode all shipped major version bumps of their top offerings, all of which have been AINews title stories in the past, but are mostly annual incremental improvements. Past guest Felix Reiseberg gets the headline today for coming out and charting the path forward for junior engineers: “Hunger beats tenure”This month, I laid the traditional coding interview to rest. As a hiring manager at Anthropic, I stopped asking candidates to do them… …There’s no more point in giving you a little React challenge than there is in quizzing people about assembly; Claude is now better at both. Our most impactful builders are successful regardless of how good they are at these tests. Enough said. His advice for juniorsPick business impact over backlog: In pre-AI-coding 2011, Patrick McKenzie wrote “engineers are hired to create business value, not to program things.” Pick a radical idea: Come up with a few ideas that would, if successful, dramatically improve the chances that your organization achieves those goals. Be ambitious! Build it over a weekend: I have seen small groups and solo engineers fly past the usual process of writing product requirements documents (PRDs), getting buy-in, and lobbying for time with designers or product managers by building a working prototype. Focus on one good idea: In my experience, junior people often make the mistake of cramming multiple ideas into a single prototype, hiding three excellent ideas among 20 bad ones. Lean into your fresh perspective: If you’re working on something user-facing, you have a unique amount of empathy for users and thus a much better sense for how the product works or doesn’t work for them. Well said, Felix! Get web search results as clean, structured Markdown, using roughly 50% fewer tokens than JSON on average. Easily integrate Markdown search results into your AI workflows across 100+ SerpApi APIs
items.why_it_matters: An Anthropic hiring manager dropping coding interviews signals shifting engineering hiring norms, relevant to how we vet staff-augmentation engineers and grow juniors.

items.title: Why Agents Love Supabase
items.author: swyx .ai
items.excerpt: I first met Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson in Singapore, shortly after they finished YC as the hottest startup of YC S20. Six years later, we finally got them on the podcast! This is their first podcast together, after taking an open-source, fully remote company from zero to a $10 billion valuation. The title is a question I wanted to understand for myself: why do agents love Supabase? There are plenty of managed databases. Postgres hosting is competitive. Being familiar to a model is useful distribution, but it doesn't explain all the work needed to turn a generated application into something that runs. But when I ran my frontier AEO tracker, it was an almost complete sweep of first choice for app backends (and in contention for managed db) for every frontier model from Astra to Fable to Muse. At Select, Supabase grouped its announcements into Build, Operate and Scale. The things that stood out to me were surprisingly practical: start a local backend without Docker, keep the desired database schema in Git, and run compute beside the database. Each removes a piece of work that developers have been doing for years. Agents make that friction harder to ignore. Watch the full conversation, including my opening commentary →Give the agent a backend it can read My favorite developer-tool announcements make me think: of course I want this today. The new alpha runtime for running Supabase locally without Docker is one of those. I use Colima rather than Docker Desktop, and even then, removing another dependency from the path to a working database is welcome. Local setup is a small part of a human developer's week; an agent that repeatedly creates and tests environments encounters it over and over. Declarative schemas are the bigger idea. The familiar SQL workflow accumulates a history: create the schema, then migrate, migrate, migrate. A declarative representation gives the agent a description of the state you want, in files it can inspect and edit alongside the application.
items.why_it_matters: Podcast with the Supabase founders on why agents favor Supabase. Useful context on our core backend and agent-generated apps, though interview-style rather than a release.

items.title: GitHub Octoverse 2026
items.excerpt: GitHub Octoverse 2026 I'm at GitHub Universe today (GitHub gave me a free ticket through their "GitHub Stars" program). EVP Jay Parikh just announced this year's Octoverse report, and highlighted these numbers in particular: This is a pretty stark representation of the impact of agentic engineering on GitHub. In 2026, merged pull requests tripled in less than a year to 220 million per month. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most of that increase in the second half of this year. New repository rate doubled this year, to 30.3 million per month. The report includes new numbers by industry, and breaks out numbers for repositories that involve "interoperability or reverse engineering". The methodology section includes notes about how they did this: Top countries by pushes to public repositories, adjusted by profile location. Pushes from each country were summed across the Octoverse year. To adjust for biases caused by VPN usage, LLM classification was used to extract the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code from the profiles of GitHub users who contributed pushes during this period [...] Industry. Public repositories created 2022 to 2026 were sorted into NAICS sectors by a fine-tuned multilingual embedding model using name, description, topics, and README, from random samples per year. [...] Interoperability. Counts public repositories created each year whose name, description, topics, or README mention interoperability or reverse engineering, or related terms, such as clean room implementation, drop-in replacement, or protocol re-implementation. Tags: github, ai, generative-ai, llms, coding-agents, disclosures, agentic-engineering
items.why_it_matters: Octoverse 2026 shows merged PRs and commits tripling from agentic engineering. A useful data point for fractional CTOs advising clients on AI-native delivery.

items.title: The October inflection point for vibe game development
items.excerpt: I've written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents - the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we've reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it's for vibe coding computer games. Tree Appreciator Emberwick Battle Drones Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove Four times as insulting What happens if someone actually puts the work in? You should build a game! Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game: 3D modeling Music generation (see Scrimshaw Jukebox) Game design (!) That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments. The challenge has been getting to a game that's actually fun to play. Game design is a deep subject area. I won't pretend to be well versed in it - I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn't think the models could do it. Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to "Make it a LOT more fun"... and it did. In the past few weeks I've vibe coded (in the classic sense of the term - no looking at the code at all) four games that I've genuinely enjoyed playing. I attended Foo Camp in Berkeley over the weekend and met several people who were having similar experiences. Building games that play well is shockingly easy now. The new challenge is coming up with concepts for games that are novel and delightful and that wouldn't exist without AI assistance. I haven't done an exhaustive study, but my current impression is that GPT-6 Astra isn't quite there yet. It can absolutely build a game, but its sense of fun doesn't match that of Opus 5.5. items.why_it_matters: New Virtual Models feature in Vercel AI Gateway, likely enabling model aliasing or routing across providers, directly relevant to LLM features we build on Vercel.

items.title: Introducing Vercel CI
items.why_it_matters: Vercel launching its own CI could overlap with or replace GitHub Actions in our Vercel-hosted Next.js pipelines; worth evaluating for build-vs-buy and client recommendations.

items.title: Agents can now enable Web Analytics and Observability Plus with Vercel CLI
items.author: Melkey Moksyakov
items.why_it_matters: Lets coding agents enable analytics and observability through Vercel CLI, useful for agent-driven setup of client Vercel projects; watch billing implications of Observability Plus.

items.title: Box Mount now runs in Vercel Sandbox
items.author: Elisabeth Rülke
items.why_it_matters: Box Mount support in Vercel Sandbox lets agent sandboxes access Box files. This is a niche feature, relevant mainly to clients building agents over Box-stored documents.

items.title: The fx adapter now runs the harness on the host
items.author: Felix Arntz
items.why_it_matters: Architecture change to fx's harness adapter separating host and sandbox; a mild security-boundary note but fx is not core to our workflow.

items.title: fx is now available in T3 Code
items.author: Andrew Gadzik
items.why_it_matters: Integration of Vercel's fx into T3 Code, a niche editor outside our core Claude Code and Codex workflow; limited direct impact.

items.title: Particle-1 is now available on AI Gateway
items.why_it_matters: A new model becomes routable via AI Gateway; unknown provider and capability make it low priority unless it proves coding-relevant.

items.title: Run Paseo agents on Vercel Sandbox
items.author: Elisabeth Rülke
items.why_it_matters: Adds another agent runtime to Vercel Sandbox, relevant to isolated execution of agent-generated code on our hosting platform, though Paseo is not a tool we use.

items.title: Vercel CI is now in beta
items.why_it_matters: Vercel launches a CI product in beta. It could overlap with or replace parts of our GitHub Actions pipelines on Vercel-hosted client projects, so it is worth evaluating.

items.title: Vercel Container Registry now supports 2 GB compressed image layers
items.author: Andy Waller
items.why_it_matters: Vercel Container Registry raises compressed layer limit to 2 GB, a minor platform change that helps teams shipping larger container images, such as ML workloads, on Vercel.

items.title: Vercel Plugin now available in OpenCode
items.author: Vincent Voyer
items.why_it_matters: Vercel plugin for OpenCode, an agentic coding tool adjacent to but not part of our Claude Code and Codex stack.

items.title: Virtual models now available on AI Gateway
items.why_it_matters: Virtual models on AI Gateway may simplify model aliasing, routing or fallback across Anthropic, OpenAI and Google APIs for client LLM features on Vercel.

items.title: AI for Science expands to foundations and research institutions
items.why_it_matters: Anthropic program expansion for scientific foundations and research institutions; a partnership announcement with little direct impact on client software delivery.

items.title: GitHub Actions Native Egress Firewall vs. Harden-Runner: Five Differences That Matter
items.excerpt: GitHub’s native egress firewall covers GitHub-hosted Linux runners. See five ways Harden-Runner goes further, from anomaly detection to build tampering
items.why_it_matters: Compares GitHub's native Actions egress firewall with Harden-Runner, relevant to securing our GitHub Actions CI pipelines against supply-chain and build tampering risks.
